studies.title: CD300f acts as an inducible inhibitory checkpoint that limits mast cell activation by suppressing MITF-dependent activation.
studies.authors: Song, Lihong, Ollé, Laia, Zhang, Zeng, Lago, Natalia et al.
studies.abstract: Mast cells (MCs) are key regulators of cutaneous immune responses and play a central role in allergic and non-IgE-mediated skin inflammation by activating the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2). The inhibitory receptor CD300f has been shown to modulate MC activation, but its role in regulating MRGPRX2-dependent signaling remains unclear. Here, we investigated CD300f expression and function in human skin MCs and its impact on MRGPRX2-mediated responses, with some comparison to IgE-mediated responses. CD300f was expressed on human skin MCs, and its surface expression increased following MRGPRX2 activation. Engagement of CD300f significantly attenuated MC activation induced by MRGPRX2-dependent stimuli, including substance P, vancomycin, and quinolone drugs. Transcriptomic analyses in CD300f-LAD2 revealed that CD300f signaling suppressed activation-associated gene programs after substance P stimulation, including NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Notably, CD300f engagement markedly downregulated microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), as confirmed at the protein level in LAD2 and skin MCs. MITF inhibition with TT012 and CD300f triggering enhance inhibitory responses, decreasing MITF and MITF-target expression more strongly. Conversely, lysyl-tRNA synthetase overexpression increases MITF expression and significantly reduces CD300f-mediated inhibition of both MRGPRX2- and FcεRI-dependent signaling. These findings reveal a CD300f-MITF regulatory axis that limits skin MC activation and inflammatory responses.

studies.title: Genetically engineering mast cells as effectors for targeted cancer cell cytotoxicity.
studies.authors: Han, Xiao, Wen, Di, Fu, Ruxing, Soto, Jennifer et al.
studies.abstract: Type-I hypersensitivity is a mast cell-mediated degranulation process induced by IgE-antigen recognition. Inspired by this highly specific mechanism, we developed a new cell therapy platform by genetically engineering mouse mast cell line MC/9 to overexpress the cytotoxic proteins perforin and granzyme B (PG-MCs) via lentiviral transduction. In the melanoma model utilizing B16 cells expressing membrane-bound OVA, a polarized degranulation of mast cells towards cancer cells was validated upon the recognition of antigens by anti-OVA IgE. PG-MCs could selectively kill cancer cells via IgE-antigen recognition. The IgE-sensitized PG-MCs administered through an intertumoral route delivered perforin 1 (Prf1) and granzyme B (Gmzb) toward target cells to potentiate anti-tumor efficacy. Moreover, we demonstrated the reprogramming effect of tumor microenvironment by PG-MC-induced hypersensitivity, driving an immune remodeling of the tumor milieu, characterized by the increased lymphocyte infiltration. In addition, this mast cell therapy, in combination with 5- fluorouracil (5-Fu), induced a significant inhibition of tumor growth in a B16-OVA mouse model, which is associated with the depletion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).

studies.title: Thiophene-Benzimidazole Conjugates Attenuate IL-33-induced Inflammation in Human Mast Cell Line and in ex vivo Human Skin Organ Cultures.
studies.authors: Gvirtz, Raanan, Kahremany, Shirin, Trifonov, Lena, Weintraub, Sagiv et al.
studies.abstract: Aberrant Interleukin-33 (IL-33) activation is associated with numerous dermatological inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, lupus, vitiligo and psoriasis. Thus, the inhibition of this pathway may provide therapeutic options in multiple pathologies. We hypothesized that targeting the IL-33 critical site of interactions with its membranal receptor, Suppression of Tumorigenicity 2 (ST2), will generate highly selective inhibitors capable of alleviating the detrimental effects of IL-33 activation. In silico-based methods for the identification of possible inhibitors of IL-33/ST2 interaction were used. Employing two structure-based pharmacophore models designed by LigandScout, a virtual screening of commercially available compounds and in house library revealed 13 compounds that may reduce level of IL-33/ST2 interaction. To verify their capacity to attenuate IL-33-induced inflammation, the compounds were tested in HMC-1.1 mast cell line and human skin slices. Two lead compounds, both thiophene-benzimidazole conjugates methyl-1-(pentan-3-yl)-2-(thiophen-2-ylmethyl)-1H-benzo[d]imidazole-5-carboxylate (LT-105) and methyl (S)-5-methyl-3-{(1-(pentan-3-yl)-2-(thiophen-2-ylmethyl)-1H-benzo[d]imidazole-5-carboxamido)}hexanoate (LT-108), were able to attenuate IL-33-induced IL-6 and IL 8 hypersecretion in pharmacological relevant concentrations. This effect correlated with reduced IL-6 and IL-8 mRNA levels, determined by RT-PCR. In addition, LT-105 and LT-108 reduced the phosphorylation of IL-33 downstream effectors; p-IRAK1 and p-P38. Further docking studies revealed possible molecular interactions of the compounds with key sites of IL-33 that are responsible for the binding with ST2. To validate the findings, the compounds were also tested in the ex vivo human skin organ culture. Both compounds LT-105 and LT-108 reduced inflammation when applied topically to the human skin samples stimulated by IL-33 in pharmacological concentrations. Our results indicate that thiophene-benzimidazole conjugates LT-105 and LT-108 can reduce IL-33 mediated inflammation both in vitro and ex vivo. Nevertheless, additional in vivo and clinical studies are required to further evaluate the ability of these compounds to treat autoimmune/inflammatory cutaneous disorders mediated by IL-33.

studies.title: Topical Remibrutinib Attenuates LL37-Induced Rosacea-Like Dermatitis by Inhibiting BTK Activation, NF-κB Signaling and Mast Cell Activation.
studies.authors: Li, Wangchao, Fan, Huiping, Liu, Hua, Ma, Qingsong et al.
studies.abstract: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder in which LL37-driven mast cell activation contributes to cutaneous inflammation. Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a key regulator of canonical IgE-dependent mast cell responses; however, its role in LL37-induced, IgE-independent mast cell activation remains unclear. This study investigated the involvement of BTK activation and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling in LL37-induced mast cell activation and evaluated the therapeutic effects of topical remibrutinib in experimental rosacea-like dermatitis. Transcriptomic data from rosacea lesions (GSE65914) were analyzed to identify dysregulated inflammatory pathways. LL37-stimulated LUVA mast cells and an LL37-induced mouse model of rosacea-like dermatitis were used for in vitro and in vivo evaluation, respectively. Cell viability, mast cell degranulation, and inflammatory mediator production were assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay (CCK-8) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). Cutaneous inflammation and dermal mast cell accumulation were evaluated by histopathological examination and toluidine blue staining. BTK and NF-κB phosphorylation were examined by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. Consistently, gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated enrichment of the NF-κB signaling pathway, with BTK included among the leading-edge genes contributing to this transcriptional signature. LL37 increased BTK and p65 phosphorylation in LUVA cells and mouse skin, accompanied by enhanced mast cell degranulation and inflammatory mediator release. Topical treatment with 1% remibrutinib reduced BTK and p65 phosphorylation, mast cell accumulation and degranulation, and inflammatory mediator levels. These changes were accompanied by reductions in erythema, epidermal thickening, and histopathological inflammation in mice. BTK and NF-κB are involved in LL37-induced, IgE-independent mast cell activation and rosacea-like inflammation. Topical remibrutinib attenuated experimental rosacea-like dermatitis by inhibiting BTK phosphorylation and NF-κB activation and mast cell activation, supporting topical BTK inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for rosacea.

studies.title: Phenotyping Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome: Clinical and Mechanistic Evidence, Candidate Biomarkers, and Implications for Management.
studies.authors: Qiao, Pengfei, Tian, Zhentao, He, Zhen
studies.abstract: Interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome are clinically overlapping conditions that should be distinguished according to Hunner lesion status. IC with Hunner lesions is a distinct inflammatory bladder disease characterized by urothelial denudation, lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, adaptive immune activation, and progressive structural impairment. The intensity and distribution of these inflammatory and structural abnormalities may vary among patients with IC, but the underlying pathological pattern is comparatively coherent. BPS without Hunner lesions is substantially more heterogeneous. Urothelial barrier dysfunction, mast cell and sensory nerve signaling, pelvic floor dysfunction, peripheral sensitization, and central or nociplastic pain mechanisms may contribute to symptoms in different combinations. Candidate urine and blood-based biomarkers, including cytokines, chemokines, neurotrophic factors, immune cell indices, and multiomics signatures, may support phenotyping, assessment of disease activity, or prediction of treatment response. However, most remain exploratory because their intended clinical use, analytical standardization, diagnostic thresholds, and external validity have not been established. This narrative review compares the clinical and histopathological features of IC and BPS, evaluates the evidence for proposed immune and neuroregulatory mechanisms, examines the translational status of candidate biomarkers, and discusses disease-specific and phenotype-guided management. These findings support a primary distinction between IC and BPS. Additional phenotyping is useful after this distinction to characterize heterogeneity within BPS and clinically relevant coexisting mechanisms.

studies.title: A Review: Mast Cells as Targets for Glucocorticoid Action.
studies.authors: Atum, Daniel, Ogwal, Jimmy Odongo, Obeny, Abel
studies.abstract: This review aims to summarize the established and potential targets of glucocorticoids (GCs) on mast cells, which are implicated in the pathophysiology of various allergic and inflammatory diseases including asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis. We sought to answer the following questions: (1) How do glucocorticoids inhibit the release of mediators from mast cells? (2) What are the effects of glucocorticoids on mast cell signaling molecules? (3) By what mechanisms do glucocorticoids induce mast cell apoptosis? and (4) What are the genomic and non-genomic mechanisms underlying these effects? Evidence published since 2020 reinforces that glucocorticoid effects on mast cells are context dependent rather than uniform. Dexamethasone can directly suppress selected functions of human and murine mast cells, including in combination with inhibitory CD300a signaling [22]. Conversely, activated human lung mast cells can reduce corticosteroid responsiveness in neighboring airway smooth muscle cells by altering glucocorticoid-regulated transcription [23]. In patients with asthma, six weeks of inhaled budesonide reduced airway mast cell infiltration and improved airway hyperresponsiveness; importantly, associations differed according to mast cell phenotype, airway location, and inflammatory phenotype [25]. Single-cell studies now reveal multiple human mast cell transcriptional states across tissues [7, 8], while integrated RNA-seq and H3K27ac profiling in primary human mast cells demonstrates selective regulation of mast-cell identity genes and super-enhancer networks [92]. These findings place glucocorticoid responsiveness within a framework of mast cell state, tissue niche, species, glucocorticoid compound, and experimental context. Glucocorticoid-associated mast cell depletion may involve reduced stromal/fibroblast-derived SCF and, in IL-3-dependent murine models, reduced IL-3 receptor expression; these are mechanistically distinct effects. Glucocorticoids can target mast cells at several levels, including mediator synthesis and release, intracellular signaling, survival, and transcriptional regulation, but the magnitude and nature of these effects vary substantially among species, tissue compartments, mast cell phenotypes/states, glucocorticoid compounds, activation pathways, and experimental conditions. Classical GR-dependent transcription involves GRE-dependent regulation and interactions with transcription factors such as NF-κB and AP-1, yet mast-cell-specific GR-regulated gene and chromatin programs remain incompletely defined. Rapid effects on degranulation are also unresolved, with evidence for membrane-associated classical GR signaling as well as other rapid mechanisms. Contemporary human and single-cell data therefore argue against treating mast cells as a single uniformly corticosteroid-responsive population. Future studies should define the molecular basis of rapid glucocorticoid signaling and map GR-responsive transcriptional and chromatin programs across primary human mast cell states and tissue niches.

studies.title: Noninvasive urinary biomarkers 3-bromotyrosine and leukotriene E4 in assessing asthma control and flare-up in children: a case-control study.
studies.authors: Yadav, Krishna Kumar, Gupta, Nitesh R, Yadav, Sunita, Kulshrestha, Manish Raj et al.
studies.abstract: To assess urinary biomarkers 3-bromotyrosine and leukotriene E4 (LTE4) levels in children with asthma and their association with asthma control and flare-up. This was a prospective study which applied a case-control design with 2:1 ratio. Children aged 3 to 15 years diagnosed with asthma according to the GINA 2022 guidelines were included. Measurements of urinary 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4 values were done using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. The asthma group (n = 146) had significantly higher urinary 3-bromotyrosine levels (22.58 ± 8.15 ng/mg creatinine) compared to healthy controls (n = 73) (14.53 ± 1.27 ng/mg creatinine, p < 0.001). Children with asthma flare-up exhibited significantly higher urinary 3-bromotyrosine levels (32.14 ± 7.76 ng/mg creatinine) compared to those with well-controlled asthma (17.16 ± 5.48 ng/mg creatinine, p < 0.001). Levels of 3-bromotyrosine decreased significantly after symptom control in hospitalized flare-up cases. Similarly, urinary LTE4 levels were significantly higher in the asthma group (308.40 ± 90.13 pg/mg creatinine) than controls (84.54 ± 18.27 pg/mg creatinine, p < 0.001). A significant difference in LTE4 levels was observed between well-controlled and flare-up cases. Urinary LTE4 levels also decreased following symptom control in hospitalized children. Both 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4 levels showed similar patterns of increase and decrease across asthma subgroups (well-controlled and flare-up). The Pearson's correlation coefficient between 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4 was r = 0.58 (p < 0.001). The ROC curve analysis demonstrated that both biomarkers moderately predict severity of asthma. The area under the curve for predicting flare-up was higher for LTE4. Noninvasive urinary biomarkers, 3-bromotyrosine, and LTE4 were elevated in asthma and flare-up. Both biomarkers exhibited similar trends, with levels rising or falling according to asthma control status. The area under the curve to severity of asthma was higher for LTE4. • Asthma in children is associated with airway inflammation; several inflammatory biomarkers correlate with disease activity. Non-invasive biomarkers are increasingly preferred in children because blood sampling and invasive procedures can be difficult. • Urinary biomarkers have been investigated in asthma, particularly markers related to oxidative stress, leukotriene metabolism, eosinophilic inflammation, and mast-cell activation. • Demonstrates that both non-invasive urinary biomarkers, 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4, are significantly elevated in children with asthma compared with healthy controls, and their higher levels are associated with poor disease control and flare-up. Both 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4, levels showed similar patterns of increase and decrease across asthma subgroups. • The Pearson's correlation coefficient between 3-bromotyrosine and LTE4 was r=0.58. The area under the curve to severe flare-up was higher for LTE4. Biomarker levels decline after symptom control provides evidence that these markers reflect ongoing disease activity and might be useful in disease monitoring.

studies.title: Hsp90 inhibitor 17-AAG reduces skin inflammation and inhibits NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome activation in DNCB-induced mice and TNF-α/IFN-γ-induced keratinocytes.
studies.authors: Chen, Yuan-Yuan, Lin, Xiao-Xiao
studies.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) represents the most common inflammatory skin condition with a high burden of disease persistence and relapse. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of 17-AAG, a Hsp90 inhibitor, in inhibiting skin inflammation in AD and its effect on nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB)/NOD-like receptor thermal protein domain associated protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome pathway. Topical application of 17-AAG was found to significantly improve inflammatory skin lesions, reduce epidermal thickness and mast cell infiltration, and decrease levels of proinflammatory cytokines in mice with AD-like skin lesions induced by using 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (1 % and 0.5 % DNCB). A reduced extent of p65 phosphorylation with declined protein expressions of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the dorsal skin lesions of 17-AAG-treated AD mice compared to vehicle-treated AD mice. In HaCaT cells inflamed by tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α)/interferon γ (IFN-γ), 17-AAG treatment significantly reduced the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, reduce the phosphorylation of p65, and decreased the protein expressions of NLRP3 and caspase-1. These results prove Hsp90 inhibitor 17-AAG could reduce skin inflammation and inhibit NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome activation in DNCB-induced mice and TNF-α/IFN-γ-induced human keratinocytes.

studies.title: Mast cell activation syndromes in clinical practice: diagnostic challenges, phenotypes, and real-life management.
studies.authors: Katran, Zeynep Yegin, Argın, Özge, Erdem, Simge, Bulut, İsmet
studies.abstract: Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) is characterized by recurrent, systemic episodes of mast cell mediator release, often resembling anaphylaxis and involving multiple organ systems. To describe clinical, laboratory, and therapeutic characteristics of patients with non-clonal mast cell activation syndromes in a real-life cohort. This retrospective study included 21 adult patients fulfilling criteria for non-clonal mast cell activation syndromes, evaluated between 2015 and 2025 at a tertiary allergy and immunology centre in Istanbul, Türkiye. Demographic features, clinical manifestations, laboratory findings, and treatment responses were analysed. Eighteen (85.7%) patients were female, with a mean age of 50.1 years. All experienced recurrent acute cutaneous symptoms, with gastrointestinal (42.9%), cardiovascular (61.9%), and respiratory (76.2%) involvement. Baseline serum tryptase levels were normal or mildly elevated, and all patients demonstrated an event-related "20% + 2 ng/ml" increase during follow-up. KIT D816V mutation was negative in peripheral blood in all patients and in bone marrow in 6 evaluated cases. No aberrant mast cell immunophenotype was detected in those undergoing bone marrow assessment. Based on available evaluation, 6 patients were classified as consistent with idiopathic (non-clonal) MCAS, whereas the remaining patients had comorbidities suggestive of secondary MCAS. Non-clonal mast cell activation syndromes remain diagnostically challenging and often require longitudinal evaluation. Omalizumab may serve as an effective adjunct therapy in patients with persistent symptoms. A phenotype-based approach is warranted.

studies.title: Outcome selection and reporting transparency in ClinicalTrials.gov-registered chronic spontaneous urticaria trials: a registry-publication linkage study.
studies.authors: Liu, Yannan, Gao, Ruhong, Peng, Yongjun, Ma, Wenli et al.
studies.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria/chronic idiopathic urticaria (CSU/CIU) trials increasingly evaluate biologics and targeted mast-cell therapies. Whether ClinicalTrials.gov-registered trials consistently capture patient-centred outcomes and disseminate results in a timely and linkable manner remains uncertain. To map registered outcome domains, patient-centred outcome breadth and reporting transparency among interventional CSU/CIU trials in ClinicalTrials.gov. ClinicalTrials.gov was searched using three CSU/CIU-related queries, yielding 486 records and 168 unique NCT registrations after deduplication. Eligible interventional trials were coded for intervention category, trial purpose and nine registered outcome domains. A descriptive 0-8 patient-centred outcome score excluded safety. A stratified sample was independently recoded by a second author. Completed or terminated trials underwent manual registry-publication linkage, with primary and secondary publications distinguished and reporting assessed at 12, 24 and 36 months after primary completion using a fixed data lock of 1 June 2026. We included 128 eligible trials; 83 were completed or terminated. Disease activity/UAS7 (78.1%), itch/pruritus (65.6%) and wheals/hives (59.4%) were commonly registered, whereas urticaria control/UCT (28.1%), angioedema (30.5%), relapse/remission/rescue medication (24.2%) and explicit sleep/daily activity (7.8%) were less frequent. The mean patient-centred score was 3.37 (SD 1.98), and 20 trials (15.6%) scored at least 6. Independent second coding showed 90.4% agreement across 270 domain-level decisions. Among 83 completed/terminated trials, 32 (38.6%) had both posted results and a confirmed primary publication, whereas 15 (18.1%) had no qualifying public result identified. Any qualifying public result was available within 12, 24 and 36 months for 18.8%, 53.5% and 66.7% of trials with sufficient follow-up, respectively. ClinicalTrials.gov-registered CSU/CIU trials show substantial heterogeneity in patient-centred outcome coverage. Distinguishing trial purpose, primary from secondary publications and reporting opportunity over time provides a more cautious assessment of the registered evidence base and highlights opportunities for more harmonised outcome selection and clearer result dissemination.

studies.title: Cell-intrinsic steroidogenesis regulates mast cell function.
studies.authors: Pramanik, Jhuma, Zhao, Qiuchen, Chakraborty, Soura, Yamashita-Kanemaru, Yumi et al.
studies.abstract: Steroid hormones are well-known regulators of mast cell function, but whether mast cells themselves produce steroids de novo and influences their effector function has remained unknown. Here, we show that mast cells constitutively express the steroidogenic enzyme cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily A member 1 (Cyp11a1) and produce pregnenolone. Cyp11a1 expression was detected across tissue-resident mast cells from multiple organs, was conserved in human mast cells, and was enhanced by interleukin-3 signaling and after activation. We identified Cyp11a1 as a Gata2-dependent, superenhancer-associated mast cell gene, placing steroidogenesis within the core mast cell transcriptional program. Loss of Cyp11a1 altered transcriptomic and proteomic programs in mast cells, with effects on pathways linked to cell growth, immune signaling, and effector function. Functionally, Cyp11a1-deficient mast cells showed increased degranulation in response to both immunoglobulin E (IgE)-dependent and IgE-independent stimulation. In vivo, loss of Cyp11a1 reduced mast cell abundance in several tissues but exacerbated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis. These findings identify cell-intrinsic steroidogenesis as a regulatory pathway that restrains mast cell activation and anaphylactic responses.

studies.title: Alcohol-Induced Hypersensitivity: A Clinical and Mechanistic Overview.
studies.journal: The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice
studies.authors: Bhatnagar, Saheba, Miyashiro, Dayna, Canty, Ethan, Woessner, Katharine et al.
studies.abstract: Patients with reactions to alcohol pose a diagnostic challenge for allergists, since such symptoms can represent true hypersensitivity, alcohol as a cofactor for other allergens, or entirely separate mimicking conditions. The literature on this topic is limited, with much of the current understanding drawn from case reports, small case series, and mechanistic studies rather than large scale trials. Although the underlying mechanism is not fully understood, several pathways have been proposed to explain this cofactor effect, which this review will discuss in detail. Alcohol has also been identified as a direct trigger of IgE-mediated, non-IgE-mediated, and delayed hypersensitivity reactions, and can exacerbate pre-existing atopic and mast cell-related conditions, including aspirin-exacerbated disease, mastocytosis and urticaria. This review provides a comprehensive overview of these mechanisms and the clinical spectrum of alcohol-related reactions, highlights key mimickers relevant to the allergist, and provides a practical framework for diagnostic evaluation.

studies.title: Immediate Perioperative Hypersensitivity and Anaphylaxis in Neuroanesthesia Practice: A Focused Review.
studies.authors: Manlapaz, Mariel, Farag, Ehab
studies.abstract: Perioperative hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon but potentially catastrophic. Neurosurgical and spine patients are especially vulnerable, as the injured brain and spinal cord tolerate anaphylaxis-induced hypotension poorly, cerebral and spinal perfusion may fall precipitously, and draping of the head and torso may obscure cutaneous signs. These procedures also rely heavily on topical hemostatic agents. National audits estimate the incidence of perioperative anaphylaxis at roughly 1 in 5000 to 10,000 anesthetics, but estimates vary geographically. No study has reported a denominator-based incidence confined to neurosurgery, leaving the true burden uncharacterized for this surgical specialty. This focused review summarizes the agents, mechanisms, and perioperative implications of immediate hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis relevant to neuroanesthesia. Immediate reactions are immunologic (IgE-mediated, or IgG- and complement-mediated) or nonimmunologic (direct mast-cell activation) but converge on mast-cell and basophil mediator release, which renders their presentations largely indistinguishable. We examine agents of relevance to neurosurgery, including neuromuscular blocking agents, cefazolin and other β-lactams, chlorhexidine, sugammadex, gelatin-based and other hemostatic agents, protamine, tranexamic acid, fluorescent and dye agents, and iodinated contrast media-alongside their mechanisms and safer alternatives. Management follows international consensus recommendations centered on prompt epinephrine administration and fluid resuscitation titrated to severity. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are useful adjuncts but should not delay resuscitation. Improved outcomes depend on greater awareness, careful allergy assessment and appropriate de-labeling, surgical-anesthesia communication, and wider access to testing and dedicated surveillance.

studies.title: Inflammatory memory as a potential driver of rosacea pathogenesis: integrating mechanisms of chronic relapse and perspectives on disease modification.
studies.authors: Zhang, Ming, Zhou, Zhou, Zhan, Dandan, Yang, Yumeng et al.
studies.abstract: Inflammatory memory refers to functional changes retained by a tissue after an inflammatory episode that allow faster or stronger responses to subsequent challenges. It encompasses epigenetic memory in epithelial and stem cells, trained immunity, and tissue-resident memory T cells. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent flushing, persistent erythema, and papulopustular lesions, and relapse after treatment cessation is common; the mechanisms that drive recurrence remain unclear. In this hypothesis-generating critical review, we use inflammatory memory as an integrative framework and examine evidence consistent with inflammatory memory in rosacea, including the Toll-like receptor 2/kallikrein-related peptidase 5/cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (LL-37) positive feedback axis, mast-cell-mediated amplification, neuroimmune amplification, and an interleukin-1β-centered persistent inflammatory program. We draw on mechanistic evidence from psoriasis and atopic dermatitis related to tissue-resident memory T cells, epithelial memory, and trained immunity, while explicitly separating established rosacea-specific observations from indirect cross-disease parallels and speculative claims. A multilayer memory network model is proposed in which repeated triggers write memory and lower the relapse threshold; disease modification is then discussed as a candidate therapeutic goal, together with potential strategies and testable hypotheses. Direct molecular evidence for inflammatory memory in rosacea is still lacking, alternative mechanisms remain plausible, and disease modification should be viewed as a perspective rather than an established endpoint.

studies.title: A pathway to next-generation mast cell stabilizers identified through the novel Phytomedical Analytics for Research Optimization at scale data platform.
studies.authors: Jansen, C, Rice, B G, Wooton, B, Howard, J et al.
studies.abstract: Mast cell stabilizers (MCS) have the potential to address unmet therapeutic need in allergy and inflammation management. MCS chronically suppress all arms of the pro-inflammatory mast cell response to stimulation (e.g., histamine, protease, lipid mediators, cytokines and chemokines). They may therefore outperform approaches such as H1, H2 and H4 inhibitors (antihistamines), which block only the acute histamine release by mast cells and leave the rest of the functional response untouched. Despite their potential, current MCS (e.g., cromolyn sodium, tranilast, nedocromil) in clinical use are hindered by poor bioavailability, frequent dosing, long lags to onset of relief, and enigmatic mechanisms of action. MCS have their origins in phytomedicine: cromolyn sodium is the longest standing drug in the class and is a derivatized form of khellin from We report a novel data analytics workflow starting with a newly developed plant-based pharmacopeia data platform with >3.5B linkage pathways (country → medical system → formulation → indication → ingredient organism → chemical component → other parameters), covering 22 M sq. miles of biogeography and historical and contemporary timeframes. Additional data layers include druggability indices, target and pathway analyses. The current study validates a subset of candidate phytomedical ngMCS using This proof-of-concept study may have particular relevance for complex presentations such as Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) where ngMCS may outperform current management approaches.

studies.title: The Role of Systemic Inflammatory Ratios in Refractory Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria Patients with Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.
studies.journal: Medical journal of the Islamic Republic of Iran
studies.authors: Bamedi, Mohammad Sina, Ansari, Hossein, Alijani, Ebrahim, Shahriari, Hossein et al.
studies.abstract: Refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria (R-CSU) is characterized by systemic mast-cell-driven inflammation, which may present with extra-cutaneous conditions such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The utility of simple blood-derived inflammatory ratios that characterize this systemic inflammation is currently limited. We investigated the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), eosinophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (ELR), and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) as potential inflammatory markers in patients with R-CSU, both with and without GERD. A retrospective case-control study was conducted involving 116 patients with recurrent chronic spontaneous urticaria (R-CSU) between 2023 and 2024 at Ali ibn Abi Talib Hospital in Zahedan. Among these patients, 58 were diagnosed with GERD, while the remaining 58 were not. Initially, GERD was clinically confirmed, after which complete blood count (CBC) parameters were utilized to calculate the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), eosinophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (ELR), and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR). Group differences were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U tests and multivariate regression, adjusted for potential confounders. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was employed to assess diagnostic accuracy. NLR was significantly higher in R-CSU patients with GERD compared to those without GERD (NLR: 2.05 ± 1.7 vs 1.05 ± 0.91, Elevated NLR and ELR indicate systemic inflammation in patients with refractory CSU and GERD. These findings support the hypothesis that systemic inflammation contributes to extracutaneous symptoms in this population. Routine, readily available CBC-derived ratios may serve as cost-effective markers for identifying systemic inflammatory activity in R-CSU.

studies.title: A trial of exosome rich stem cell secretome as a potential treatment for Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
studies.authors: Flynn, Kevin J, Ransom, John T, McGrath, Daniel
studies.abstract: Hypermobile Type Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) accounts for 80%-90% of all Ehlers-Danlos cases. hEDS pathophysiology is uncertain. There is no diagnostic test. Symptoms include joint hypermobility, intractable and debilitating joint pain, chronic fatigue, brain fog, irritable bowel symptoms and mast cell activation syndrome. Treatment options are limited and ineffective. None are disease-modifying. This pilot study evaluated the safety and potential for efficacy of a novel biologic investigational product (IP) comprising an extracellular vesicle enriched secretome from human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (hbm-MSC EVs). Ten (10) hEDS patients were recruited and treated with up to four doses of IP by intravenous infusion for up to five months. Symptoms were assessed using a custom 9-criteria questionnaire addressing common symptoms and by observation at each infusion. No treatment related adverse events were reported or noted. Statistically significant response was found before treatment and after treatment for the ten patients as a group. However, six (6) out of the ten (10) patient exhibited distinct, substantial, rapid, and sustained overall improvement of their symptoms within the study time frame. Due to time limitations of the study, a single distinct responder (one of six responders), with IND approval for continued treatment, was further treated and observed for an additional twelve (12) months. Treatment was ultimately stopped at the patient's request and for 32 months thereafter has lived in apparent remission without pain or any previous symptoms or signs of Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome. All five (5) prior distinct responders with discontinued treatment reverted to their pre-treatment condition. Results of this pilot study suggest that a randomized, controlled trial is warranted to evaluate the potential of the IP for treatment of hEDS.

studies.title: Sensory innervation shapes cancer immunotherapy efficacy and adverse events.
studies.authors: Adamczyk, Natalie S, Saloman, Jami L, Scheff, Nicole N
studies.abstract: Sensory neurons innervate the tumor microenvironment (TME) and are active contributors to tumor progression and immune evasion. Across multiple cancer types, higher intratumoral nerve density is associated with worse clinical outcomes, including increased lymph node metastasis, local recurrence, and reduced survival. This relationship is driven, at least in part, by local immunosuppression arising from neuropeptide and neurotransmitter paracrine signaling within the TME. Nociceptive sensory neurotransmission impacts tumor-infiltrating immune cells to promote T-cell exhaustion, mast cell degranulation, and stromal remodeling, collectively constructing a barrier to effective antitumor immunity. Beyond paracrine signaling, sensory neurons themselves express immune checkpoint proteins, including programmed cell death ligand-1, providing an additional mechanism by which the sensory nervous system participates in local immune regulation. Preclinical studies have established that targeting sensory neuron signaling, whether through denervation, neuropeptide antagonism, or axon guidance inhibition, can relieve TME immunosuppression and improve the efficacy of immune-based therapies. Several Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved agents developed for non-oncologic indications, including calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonists approved for migraine, and the NK-1R antagonist Aprepitant, represent immediately available candidates for repurposing in combination immunotherapy strategies. The relationship between sensory neurons and immunotherapy is bidirectional; however, immunotherapies also act on sensory neurons, and this interaction likely contributes to the development and severity of immune-related adverse events through disruption of constitutive neuronal checkpoint signaling and neurogenic amplification of tissue inflammation. Sensory neurons in densely innervated barrier organs may serve as neuroimmune amplifiers that worsen the severity of colitis, pneumonitis, and dermatitis during checkpoint blockade. This review examines the evidence for how sensory neural signaling shapes immunotherapy efficacy, and how immunotherapies impinge on sensory neuron biology to promote adverse events. Throughout, we highlight translational opportunities where modulation of the sensory nervous system may improve therapeutic outcomes or reduce treatment toxicity.

studies.title: Systemic Allergic Reactions to mRNA COVID-19 Vaccines: A Randomized Placebo-controlled Trial.
studies.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
studies.authors: Wheatley, Lisa M, Baker, James R, Adkinson, N Franklin, Gruchalla, Rebecca et al.
studies.abstract: COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were associated in early reports with more allergic reactions than most vaccines, especially in people with allergic histories. To estimate the proportions of systemic allergic reactions to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in people reporting prior severe allergic reactions to various allergens, and/or mast cell disorders (PSAR/MCD Group) and determine if proportions are higher than in non-PSAR/non-MCD (Comparison Group). We conducted a multi-center, randomized, double-blinded (for the initial injection), placebo-controlled trial in PSAR/MCD vs Comparison adults and adolescents. Participants received a double-blinded injection with Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or placebo, followed by unblinded vaccine injections. The primary outcome was the incidence of clinically-determined systemic allergic reactions within 90 minutes after injection. The trial enrolled 723 participants of a planned 3400, with 664 (56% PSAR/MCD) receiving at least one injection. Within 90 minutes of injection, systemic allergic reactions occurred in 5/180 (3%) PSAR/MCD participants given Pfizer-BioNTech (vs 0/133 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.063) and 2/173 (1%) PSAR/MCD participants given Moderna (vs 0/144 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.27). Reactions were also reported >90 minutes and ≤48 hours only in PSAR/MCD. Among PSAR/MCD participants, reaction rates to vaccine within 90-minutes and 48-hours were similar to placebo. Extensive laboratory studies did not identify plausible reaction mechanisms. Systemic allergic reactions based solely on clinical determination within 90-minutes or 48-hours of vaccination were only observed in PSAR/MCD but failure to achieve planned enrollment limited statistical precision. Reactions to placebo and failure to identify underlying immunologic mechanisms suggest non-allergic or non-immunologic causes.

studies.title: Type I autoimmunity in chronic spontaneous urticaria: Evidence, limits, and endotype overlap.
studies.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
studies.authors: Konstantinou, George N, Grattan, Clive E H
studies.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a mast cell-driven disorder with basophil involvement and several possible upstream mechanisms. Type IIb autoimmune CSU, mediated by functional IgG autoantibodies against FcεRIα or IgE, is the best-validated endotype. Evidence for type I autoimmune (autoallergic) CSU is less complete, but findings involving IgE autoantibodies to thyroid peroxidase (TPO), IL-24, and other self-antigens suggest that IgE-dependent autoreactivity may be relevant in some patients. However, total IgE level, atopy, allergic disease, and timing of the response to omalizumab are not diagnostic of this mechanism. Rather than viewing type I and type IIb CSU as competing categories, we hypothesize 2 potentially overlapping immunologic axes: an IgE-autoantibody axis and an IgG/complement axis. Patients may lie closer to one axis, show markers of both, or remain provisionally idiopathic because current biomarkers cannot classify them with confidence. Progress will require harmonized functional assays; skin, mast cell, and basophil readouts, as well as longitudinal treatment studies. The central question is when an IgE autoantibody is only a passenger, when it is a partner, and when it is the driver of the wheal.

studies.title: Estradiol-associated extracellular signaling in the human breast
studies.authors: Abrahamsson, Annelie, Wang, Xingyue, Zhong, Wen, Dabrosin, Charlotta

Novel therapeutics for prevention and treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer are needed. Cell-cell interactions within the microenvironment contribute to breast cancer progression through extracellular signaling. studies.title: [Beyond the placebo effect: exploring the mast cell-dependent analgesic effect of shallow needling control].
studies.journal: Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion
studies.authors: Luo, Zhengrong, Zhang, Youwen, Ge, Xiaolei, Tian, Xinyi et al.
studies.abstract: Based on the distribution characteristics of mast cells and existing mechanistic evidence, the study explores the potential biological effects of shallow needling control (sham-acupuncture). Regarding cellular distribution, mast cells exhibit a physiological characteristic of dense distribution in both the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, predominantly in the distal regions, and show a higher density in acupoint areas compared with non-acupoint areas. At the puncture site, shallow needling primarily targets the dermis and the superficial subcutaneous tissue, with these two layers overlapping anatomically. Regarding its mechanism of action, acupuncture can induce local mast cell degranulation through mechanical stimulation, thereby releasing bioactive substances that subsequently activate relevant signaling pathways to produce analgesic effect. The study proposes that the shallow needling control at the same acupoint or non-acupoint not merely obtains placebo effect, but also involves potential biological mechanism associated with mast cells, aiming to provide new insights for future clinical trial design and research on the underlying mechanism of acupuncture and sham-acupuncture. 基于肥大细胞的分布特点和现有机制证据，探讨浅刺对照（假针刺）的潜在生物学效应。在细胞分布上，肥大细胞具有在真皮层与皮下组织层分布密集，以远心端为主、穴位区较非穴区更为丰富的生理特点；在刺入位置上，浅刺对照主要涉及皮肤真皮层和皮下浅层，二者于解剖层面重叠。在作用机制上，针刺可通过机械刺激促使局部肥大细胞脱颗粒，释放生物活性物质，进而激活相关信号通路产生镇痛效应。提出以同穴或非穴浅刺为主的针刺对照不仅仅是安慰剂效应，还存在与肥大细胞相关的潜在生物学效应，以期为未来针刺与假针刺的临床试验设计及效应机制研究提供新的思路。.

studies.title: Luteolin alleviates neurogenic inflammation in OVA-induced combined allergic rhinitis and asthma syndrome mice through TRPV1/ERK-related signaling.
studies.journal: International archives of allergy and immunology
studies.authors: Li, Jing, Mirodilova, Firuza, Lei, Lei
studies.abstract: Combined Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma Syndrome (CARAS), a common chronic allergic respiratory disease, involves dysregulated neuro-immune interactions and neurogenic inflammation. Luteolin (LUT) has significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. However, its effects and underlying mechanism in CARAS remain unclear. This study aims to determine the effects of LUT administration during the airway challenge phase of CARAS and its association with TRPV1/ERK signaling. BALB/C mice were used to establish an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced CARAS model and LUT was administered. The nasal symptoms were evaluated by counting the number of nasal scratching and sneezing. HE and toluidine blue staining were performed to determine the histopathological changes. Total and differential cell counts in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were determined. The levels of histamine, MCP-1, substance P (SP), CGRP and Th1/Th2/Th17-related cytokines were detected by ELISA kit. Besides, TRPV1 and p-ERK expression levels were measured by immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting. Our study indicated that LUT administration significantly reduced sneezing frequency, nasal scratching behavior, and serum OVA-specific IgE level in CARAS mice compared to the model group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated that LUT administration reduced inflammatory cell accumulation and histological scores in the nasal mucosa and lung tissues and was associated with reduced inflammatory cell counts in BALF. In addition, LUT administration reduced mast cell density in both tissues. Serum histamine and MCP-1 levels and pulmonary levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-17A, and IFN-γ were also reduced following LUT administration. LUT administration also reduced serum and BALF levels of SP and CGRP. Furthermore, LUT administration reduced TRPV1 expression and p-ERK levels in the nasal mucosa and lung tissue. LUT administration attenuates allergic and inflammatory responses in OVA-induced CARAS mice, which may be associated with TRPV1/ERK signaling.

studies.title: LL-37-MRGPRX2-Mast Cell Signaling in Rosacea: Current Evidence and Directions for Human Studies.
studies.authors: Yin, Haoyang, Lu, Yiping
studies.abstract: This critical narrative review examines evidence relevant to LL-37-Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2)-mast-cell signaling in rosacea and considers the relevance of these findings to future human studies. Literature was identified through PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection searches, supplemented by examination of reference lists from relevant original studies and recent reviews. Human rosacea tissue studies show changes in mast-cell abundance or degranulation-associated staining and localize MRGPRX2 to lesional mast cells. Human mast-cell and receptor studies demonstrate LL-37-responsive MRGPRX2 calcium signaling and degranulation and show pharmacological inhibition of MRGPRX2-mediated responses. LL-37-induced mouse models support contributions of mast cells and murine Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor member B2 (MrgprB2), although human MRGPRX2 and murine MrgprB2 are pharmacologically distinct. Other LL-37-responsive pathways and downstream regulatory processes may also produce or modify similar mast-cell outcomes. Direct selective functional testing of MRGPRX2 in patients with rosacea remains lacking, and receptor-level functional findings and patient-level observations still arise largely from different study settings. Future human studies could therefore connect lesional MRGPRX2 status and selective receptor perturbation with proximal mast-cell responses and corresponding tissue or clinical changes within the same rosacea study setting. Under adequately designed study conditions, concordant findings may strengthen support for MRGPRX2 involvement, whereas partial, discordant, subgroup-restricted, or absent proximal responses may help refine its functional scope in human rosacea.

studies.title: Inducible Laryngeal Obstruction in Hypermobile Patients.
studies.authors: Menton, Stacey M, Fairweather, DeLisa, Wilson, Frances C, Zangerle, Derek J et al.
studies.abstract: To determine whether patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) have more voice, cough, swallowing, GI issues, and MC activation than patients without ILO. This retrospective study of 2162 patients meeting 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS (n = 507) or HSD (n = 1655) who were seen at the EDS Clinic in Mayo Clinic Florida from November 2019 to June 2025 compared patients who screened positive for ILO to those who screened negative. Patients were examined for self-reported symptoms of voice, cough, swallow, and GI issues as well as MC activation. Among patients with hEDS or HSD, 23.1% and 17.1% respectively screened positive for ILO. Patients with ILO had significantly more voice, cough, and swallow issues than patients without ILO (all p ≤ 0.007). Both diagnoses had more gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) (hEDS: 55.6% vs. 40.9%, p = 0.004; HSD: 55.8% vs. 42.2%, p < 0.0001). Additionally, both hEDS and HSD patients with ILO self-reported 18 allergy-related symptoms more often than those without ILO and had higher MC scores indicating widespread MC activation (all p < 0.0001). Cough, dysphagia, and elevated MC score were statistically significant predictors of ILO in both hEDS and HSD within a logistic regression analysis. Chronic cough, dysphagia, and elevated MC symptom burden were the strongest independent predictors of ILO across both hEDS and HSD, underscoring the need for routine multidisciplinary laryngeal assessment in this population.

studies.title: Food-Associated Kounis Syndrome: Clinical Spectrum and Diagnostic Considerations from a Case Report and Systematic Qualitative Synthesis of Published Cases.
studies.authors: Sanchez-Fernandez, Sergio, Lasarte, Gabriel Gastaminza, Garófalo, Carmen D'Amelio, Paredes-Gutierrez, Enrique et al.
studies.abstract: Kounis syndrome (KS) is a hypersensitivity-associated acute coronary syndrome. Food-associated KS remains poorly characterized, and its clinical presentation may be mimicked by non-immune food-related toxic reactions. To characterize the food exposures, clinical and cardiovascular presentations, allergological assessment, potential cofactors, KS phenotypes, management, and outcomes reported in food-associated KS. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to August 22, 2026. Original case reports, case series, and sufficiently informative conference reports describing objective coronary involvement temporally associated with a food or food-derived exposure were included. Patient-level data were synthesized qualitatively. KS diagnostic certainty, coronary phenotype, food causality, and presumed mechanism were assessed separately. Planned sensitivity analyses restricted the synthesis to confirmed or suspected food allergy, definite or probable KS, and cases without epinephrine administration before coronary onset or its first objective documentation. The synthesis included 50 publications or reports describing 53 unique patients. Food-related mechanisms comprised confirmed food allergy in 20 patients, clinically suspected food allergy in 26, scombroid poisoning in six, and a Coprinopsis atramentaria-alcohol interaction in one. The reported coronary spectrum ranged from transient vasospasm and nonobstructive presentations to plaque-related myocardial infarction, native-coronary thrombosis, and stent or graft thrombosis. Type I was the most frequently assigned phenotype. Allergological assessment, paired acute and baseline tryptase measurements, treatment chronology, and long-term follow-up were inconsistently reported. The main cardiovascular patterns remained broadly consistent across the planned sensitivity analyses. Food-associated KS encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of allergic coronary presentations. Clinically similar non-immune food-related toxic reactions, including scombroid poisoning, should be recognized as differential diagnoses and analyzed separately from true allergic KS. Diagnosis requires integration of exposure chronology, objective cardiovascular findings, coronary substrate, allergological evidence, potential cofactors, and competing exposures. Intramuscular epinephrine remains the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, and temporal precedence should not be interpreted as evidence that epinephrine caused the coronary event.

studies.title: Mast cell activation syndrome: Global perspectives from a World Allergy Organization survey on knowledge, diagnosis, and access to care.
studies.authors: Giavina-Bianchi, Pedro, Giavina-Bianchi, Mara, Morais-Almeida, Mário, Álvarez-Twose, Iván et al.
studies.abstract: Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) has emerged as a highly debated and increasingly recognized condition in allergy and clinical immunology. Despite established AIM/ECNM consensus criteria, major uncertainties persist regarding its diagnosis, implementation in real-world practice, and equitable access to diagnostic resources worldwide. To evaluate global knowledge, diagnostic practices, clinical exposure, and access to care related to MCAS among allergists and clinical immunologists, and to identify critical unmet needs contributing to diagnostic uncertainty. We conducted a cross-sectional international survey primarily involving allergists and clinical immunologists affiliated with the World Allergy Organization (WAO). The survey instrument was developed by international experts in mast cell disorders, including contributors to the conceptual framework and consensus diagnostic criteria for MCAS. The questionnaire assessed knowledge of consensus diagnostic criteria, clinical experience with suspected and confirmed MCAS, access to validated laboratory testing, diagnostic confidence, and treatment strategies. Regional comparisons were performed to identify disparities in practice patterns and resource availability. Marked global heterogeneity was observed in knowledge of MCAS diagnostic criteria, application of consensus frameworks, and access to essential laboratory testing. Across all regions, clinicians reported a substantial and consistent gap between the number of patients suspected of having MCAS and those who ultimately fulfilled all diagnostic criteria. Objective biomarker confirmation-particularly documentation of dynamic serum tryptase changes and access to urinary mast cell mediator metabolites-emerged as the principal diagnostic bottleneck worldwide. However, the imbalance between suspected and confirmed cases persisted even in regions with relatively greater laboratory access, suggesting that structural limitations coexist with potential diagnostic overextension and inconsistent clinical phenotyping. Management approaches were predominantly empiric and symptom-driven, often implemented in the absence of complete diagnostic confirmation. Respondents highlighted the need for clearer guidance, improved biomarker accessibility, and refinement of definitions to reduce diagnostic ambiguity. MCAS represents a condition in which both under-recognition and diagnostic uncertainty remain important challenges in contemporary practice. Significant unmet needs include strengthening clinician knowledge and application of the AIM/ECNM diagnostic framework, expanding global access to validated biomarkers, improving diagnostic precision, and harmonizing clinical approaches. At the same time, the findings of this survey suggest a need for continued evaluation and refinement of the current diagnostic framework to improve its applicability across the heterogeneous clinical spectrum of patients with suspected MCAS. Coordinated international efforts are urgently required to reduce diagnostic uncertainty, minimize inequities in care, and support the continued evolution toward a more accurate, consistent, and clinically applicable diagnostic approach worldwide.

studies.title: Imperatorin exerts anti-colorectal cancer effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell degranulation.
studies.journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
studies.authors: Shi, Xianpeng, Zhang, Peng, Cui, Xia, Hou, Yajing et al.
studies.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major global malignancy with a poor prognosis in advanced stages. Aberrant mast cell activation within the tumor microenvironment (TME) drives CRC progression; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumor-promoting role of mast cells in the hypoxic TME remain unclear, and effective therapies targeting these cells are lacking. To investigate the role of the NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2)-reactive oxygen species (ROS)-calcium signaling axis in mast cell activation and evaluate the anti-CRC activity of imperatorin (IMP), a natural furanocoumarin. Human mast cell and CRC cell lines were used to establish hypoxic activation and conditioned medium co-culture systems. Tissue microarrays, single‑cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets and CT26 allograft mouse models were employed, combined with gain/loss-of-function, Western Blot, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence and cell functional assays. NOX2 expression was significantly upregulated in activated mast cells from human CRC tissues. IMP inhibited NOX2, thereby blocking hypoxia-induced oxidative stress and mast cell degranulation. This intervention suppressed the secretion of tumor-promoting mediators and effectively inhibited CRC cell proliferation and invasion. Furthermore, in vivo experiments demonstrated that IMP dose-dependently suppressed CRC allograft growth in murine models without causing overt systemic toxicity. This study reveals a mechanism by which mast cells promote CRC progression in the hypoxic TME and demonstrates that IMP exerts potent anti-CRC effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell activation. These findings identify both a therapeutic target and a promising lead compound for TME-targeted CRC therapy.

studies.title: Mechanistic insight into eosinophilic enteritis and related disorders.
studies.authors: Syverson, Erin P, Venkatesh, Rajitha D, Bailey, Dominique D
studies.abstract: Eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases (EGIDs) affecting the gastrointestinal tract outside of the esophagus are categorized as non-EoE EGIDs, and knowledge regarding their natural history and pathophysiology is rapidly advancing. This review synthesizes evolving mechanistic insights in non-EoE EGID immunopathogenesis, emerging paradigms of disease development, and how these insights influence potential therapeutic options for these conditions. The prevalence of non-EoE EGIDs is rising, though overall prevalence remains much lower than that of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). Recent standardization of the nomenclature and histologic diagnostic thresholds for non-EoE EGIDs has facilitated progress in understanding the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and therapeutic targets of these conditions. Transcriptomic signatures of disease in the proximal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, and small intestine, are distinct from those in the colon, suggesting that segment-specific therapeutics may be appropriate. Mechanisms beyond eosinophilic inflammation, including mast cell activation, Th2 cytokine signaling, and structural remodeling, may also contribute to disease pathogenesis. Mechanistic insights elucidated from extensive transcriptomic studies and clinical trials have revealed the broader type 2 pathophysiology of non-EoE EGIDs, thereby offering a valuable opportunity to identify novel therapeutic targets and inform the design of future clinical trials.

studies.title: The dual and context-dependent role of mast cells in cutaneous wound healing and scar formation.
studies.authors: Kushwaha, Pooja, Mukhopadhyay, Sangita
studies.abstract: Successful tissue repair depends on the precise orchestration of phase-specific cellular responses alongside sustained activity of multifunctional immune regulators. Mast cells, which have primarily been long regarded as effector cells of allergic reactions, have emerged as pivotal modulators of wound repair. Importantly, mast cell activity exhibits a dual nature: while transient activation supports efficient repair and granulation tissue formation, sustained or excessive activation is associated with pathological fibrosis, hypertrophic scarring and keloid formation. Although many experimental studies and clinical evidences implicate a critical role for mast cells in wound repair, several key questions remain. Specifically, the contributions of distinct mast cell subtypes and the precise temporal dynamics of their mediator release, as well as the intricate molecular crosstalk between mast cells, stromal components, and other infiltrating immune cells remans a subject of active investigation. This review highlights current literature on the multifaceted roles of mast cells across the successive phases of wound-healing, and the specific mechanisms by which mast cells support or impair tissue repair, outlining unresolved questions in the field. Through this discussion, we aim to provide a framework for developing new therapeutic strategies to improve healing outcomes and facilitate better scar management.

studies.title: Mast cell degranulation damages glymphatic system via PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 to exacerbate hydrocephalus post intraventricular hemorrhage.
studies.authors: Yang, Yijian, Ouyang, Qian, Wang, Junqiang, Wang, Kaiyue et al.
studies.abstract: Hydrocephalus following intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) remains a serious neurological condition with limited treatment options beyond invasive surgical interventions, underscoring the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence implicates impaired glymphatic system function in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus, particularly through dysregulation of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expression in astrocytes, which is essential for cerebral waste clearance and fluid homeostasis. Since mast cells are key mediators of neuroinflammation and can influence cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics, this study investigated their role and underlying mechanisms in hydrocephalus following IVH. An IVH model was established in male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats by injecting autologous blood into the lateral ventricle. Rats were divided into the following groups: sham operation, IVH, IVH treated with the mast cell stabilizer disodium cromoglycate (DSCG), and IVH treated with DSCG plus the protein kinase C (PKC) activator phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA). In a rat model of IVH, mast cell degranulation and the release of tryptase and chymase were observed, accompanied by significant impairment of glymphatic influx and efflux. This dysfunction was characterized by reduced penetration of CSF tracers into the brain parenchyma and diminished clearance of interstitial solutes. Pharmacological stabilization of mast cells with DSCG substantially improved glymphatic function, restored glymphatic structural integrity, reduced ventricular enlargement, and ameliorated neurological deficits. Mechanistically, mast cell-derived proteases activated the PKC/p38MAPK signaling pathway, leading to decreased AQP4 expression and altered AQP4 distribution at astrocytic endfeet, thereby disrupting the perivascular polarization critical for glymphatic flow. This mechanism was supported by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), which demonstrated an interaction between p38MAPK and AQP4, and by rescue experiments, which showed that PKC activation reversed DSCG's protective effects. In vitro experiments conducted under indirect co-culture conditions further demonstrated the interaction between mast cells and astrocytes. Our results reveal a novel mast cell-PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 pathway in the development of hydrocephalus following IVH and identify mast cell stabilization as a promising therapeutic strategy for hydrocephalus post-IVH, offering a potential non-invasive approach to manage this devastating complication.

studies.title: From nasal cytology to cellular endotyping: mast cell-eosinophil interactions and overlapping inflammation in allergic rhinitis.
studies.authors: Gelardi, Matteo
studies.abstract: Allergic rhinitis is traditionally defined by allergen sensitization and type 2 inflammation, yet increasing evidence indicates that this framework does not fully capture the biological heterogeneity of the nasal mucosa. The local inflammatory landscape reflects a dynamic interaction among epithelial cells, innate and adaptive lymphoid populations, mast cells, eosinophils, stromal elements, and vascular components, and may diverge substantially from systemic biomarkers. Recent single-cell and multi-omic studies have further revealed disease-associated alterations in epithelial differentiation, stromal activation, and cell-cell communication, reinforcing the concept of the nasal mucosa as an integrated immunological ecosystem. Within this context, mast cell-eosinophil interactions appear particularly relevant, as their coexistence and degranulation may characterize inflammatory states that differ from isolated eosinophilia. Nasal cytology provides a clinically accessible morphological readout of this local cellular architecture and has shown that allergic rhinitis does not correspond to a single cytological expression. In some patients, established allergic sensitization coexists with recognized non-allergic cellular rhinitis entities, including non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophils (NARES), non-allergic rhinitis with mast cells (NARMA), and non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophils and mast cells (NARESMA), giving rise to the concept of overlapping rhinitis. This phenomenon challenges a binary allergic versus non-allergic classification and may contribute to difficult-to-treat disease and incomplete therapeutic responses. Although these nosological entities are clinically and cytologically defined, they should not be considered synonymous with molecular endotypes. Their future value may instead lie in a cytology-informed endotyping strategy integrating morphology with local biomarkers, proteomics, transcriptomics, and single-cell approaches. This Review discusses the cellular players and interactions shaping allergic rhinitis, the biological and clinical relevance of overlapping inflammation, and the potential role of nasal cytology as an interface between clinical phenotyping and molecular endotyping.

studies.title: Tryptase Locus Variation Contributes to Normal-Range Basal Serum Tryptase Variability and Is Associated With Anaphylaxis.
studies.journal: Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology
studies.authors: Svetina, Manca, Lyons, Jonathan J, Kopač, Peter, Šelb, Julij et al.
studies.abstract: Increased basal serum tryptase level (BST) is associated with anaphylaxis. In the absence of clonal mast cell disease and hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT), the contribution of the tryptase locus variation to BST and anaphylaxis remains undefined. To determine the impact of tryptase locus variation on BST and anaphylaxis. Individuals with systemic Hymenoptera venom allergic reactions, large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization underwent a novel ddPCR-based tryptase genotyping to quantify active tryptase alleles. Individuals positive for KIT p.D816V or HαT were excluded. The cohort consisted of 295 individuals with systemic reactions, 140 with large local reactions, and 29 asymptomatically sensitized individuals. Active tryptase allele number, excluding the inactive βIIIFS allele, correlated with BST levels (r = 0.34, p < 0.0001); all BST values were within the normal range. Patients with systemic reactions had higher BST compared with those with large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization (median, 4.5 ng/mL vs. 3.5 ng/mL; p < 0.0001). Individuals carrying four active β-tryptase alleles were less likely to experience anaphylaxis than those carrying two or three active β-tryptase alleles (26.7% vs. 42.3%; p = 0.024). A trend towards more severe reactions was observed in individuals carrying α-tryptase allele together with a higher number of active β-tryptase alleles. Variation at the tryptase locus explains differences in BST levels within the normal range. Four active β-tryptase alleles were associated with a lower frequency of anaphylaxis.

studies.title: Insulin Enhances Nitroglycerin-Induced Hyperalgesia Through Insulin-Responsive Receptor Signalling Involving the Trigeminovascular System and Meningeal Mast Cells.
studies.authors: Torun, Ibrahim Ethem, Celik, Humeyra, Kilinc, Erkan, Kurtoglu, Muhammet Guzel
studies.abstract: Migraine headache prevalence is lower in patients with diabetes, but the underlying mechanisms remains unclear. This study explored the influences of hyperglycemia, insulin and insulin receptor (IR)/insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R)-related signalling on migraine-related mechanisms in in vivo and ex vivo rat models. In in vivo experiments, migraine-relevant responses were induced by systemic injection of nitroglycerin (NTG), whereas hyperglycemia was induced by streptozotocin (STZ). The effects of hyperglycemia, insulin and the dual IR/IGF-1R inhibitor BMS-754807 were investigated. In ex vivo experiments, the effects of insulin and BMS on basal and capsaicin-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) releases from migraine-associated tissues (peripheral meningeal afferents and trigeminal ganglion, and central brainstem trigeminal nucleus) were directly tested. Mechanical hyperalgesia was evaluated by von-Frey, CGRP and c-Fos levels by ELISA and meningeal mast cells by toluidine-blue staining. In in vivo NTG group, insulin further lowered the pain threshold and further enhanced CGRP and c-fos concentrations in trigeminal tissues and mast cell activation in the meninges. Hyperglycemia alone or in the NTG-treated group did not change these parameters. In ex vivo experiments, direct administration of insulin stimulated CGRP release in meningeal and trigeminal ganglion, but not trigeminal nucleus, tissues and further enhanced capsaicin-stimulated CGRP release, confirming the in vivo effects. The in vivo and ex vivo effects of insulin were reversed by BMS. Hyperglycemia did not modify the NTG-induced responses. However, insulin facilitates migraine-related responses by enhancing trigeminal CGRP signalling and meningeal mast cell activation through IR and/or IGF-1R-related signalling. Modulation of insulin-responsive IR/IGF-1R-related signalling within the trigeminovascular system may represent a potential target for future therapeutic strategies.

studies.title: Gut Inflammation Favors Adverse Food Reactions by Disrupting the Microbial Metabolism of Food Triggers.
studies.authors: Da Luz, Bruna B, Rondeau, Liam E, Dang, Rebecca, Coppens, Dana et al.
studies.abstract: Food-related adverse reactions are frequently reported by patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. We investigated how intestinal inflammation and the microbiota contribute to the development of adverse food reactions. We sensitized mice to different foods (dairy and gluten) after intestinal inflammation (chemically and hapten-induced models), then mice were re-exposed to the sensitizing foods through diet enrichment. To study whether inflamed microbiota facilitates adverse food reactions, we used gnotobiotic models and bacterial supplementation experiments. We assessed markers of intestinal inflammation and sensitization, clinical responses, RNA transcripts, and microbiota composition and function. In a translational approach, we recruited IBD patients in remission and healthy controls, recorded self-reported food intolerances and clinical responses to triggering foods, and collected feces for gut microbiota analyses. Intestinal inflammation facilitates food sensitization by disrupting microbial antigen metabolism, recruiting mast cells to the colon, and favoring immunoglobulin E production. In gnotobiotic models, inflammation-driven depletion of colonic bacteria involved in food digestion contributed to food sensitization. Upon re-exposure to triggering foods, sensitized mice experienced visceral pain and low-grade inflammation through mast cell-mediated mechanisms, which also worsened experimental colitis. Supplementation with depleted bacteria or treatment with mast cell stabilizers attenuated food-driven responses. In IBD patients, self-reported food intolerances were common and associated with microbial disruption and depletion of food-metabolizing bacteria. Microbial metabolism of foods is disrupted after intestinal inflammation. This facilitates food sensitization, through colonic mast cell-mediated immune responses, which may explain the high number of adverse food reactions reported by IBD patients.
